content.text:
> pi can create skills. Ask it to build one for your use case.

# Skills

Skills are self-contained capability packages that the agent loads on-demand. A skill provides specialized workflows, setup instructions, helper scripts, and reference documentation for specific tasks.

Pi implements the [Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io/specification), warning about most violations but remaining lenient. Pi allows skill names to differ from their parent directory even though the standard disallows it; that rule is suboptimal for shared skill directories used across multiple agent harnesses.

## Table of Contents

- [Locations](#locations)
- [How Skills Work](#how-skills-work)
- [Skill Commands](#skill-commands)
- [Skill Structure](#skill-structure)
- [Frontmatter](#frontmatter)
- [Validation](#validation)
- [Example](#example)
- [Skill Repositories](#skill-repositories)

## Locations

> **Security:** Skills can instruct the model to perform any action and may include executable code the model invokes. Review skill content before use.

Pi loads skills from:

- Global:
  - `~/.pi/agent/skills/`
  - `~/.agents/skills/`
- Project:
  - `.pi/skills/`
  - `.agents/skills/` in `cwd` and ancestor directories (up to git repo root, or filesystem root when not in a repo)
- Packages: `skills/` directories or `pi.skills` entries in `package.json`
- Settings: `skills` array with files or directories
- CLI: `--skill <path>` (repeatable, additive even with `--no-skills`)

Discovery rules:
- In `~/.pi/agent/skills/` and `.pi/skills/`, direct root `.md` files are discovered as individual skills
- In all skill locations, directories containing `SKILL.md` are discovered recursively
- In `~/.agents/skills/` and project `.agents/skills/`, root `.md` files are ignored

Disable discovery with `--no-skills` (explicit `--skill` paths still load).

### Using Skills from Other Harnesses

To use skills from Claude Code or OpenAI Codex, add their directories to settings:

```json
{
  "skills": [
    "~/.claude/skills",
    "~/.codex/skills"
  ]
}
```

For project-level Claude Code skills, add to `.pi/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "skills": ["../.claude/skills"]
}
```

## How Skills Work

1. At startup, pi scans skill locations and extracts names and descriptions
2. The system prompt includes available skills in XML format per the [specification](https://agentskills.io/integrate-skills)
3. When a task matches, the agent uses `read` to load the full SKILL.md (models don't always do this; use prompting or `/skill:name` to force it)
4. The agent follows the instructions, using relative paths to reference scripts and assets

This is progressive disclosure: only descriptions are always in context, full instructions load on-demand.

## Skill Commands

Skills register as `/skill:name` commands:

```bash
/skill:brave-search           # Load and execute the skill
/skill:pdf-tools extract      # Load skill with arguments
```

Arguments after the command are appended to the skill content as `User: <args>`.

Toggle skill commands via `/settings` in interactive mode or in `settings.json`:

```json
{
  "enableSkillCommands": true
}
```

## Skill Structure

A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file. Everything else is freeform.

```
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md              # Required: frontmatter + instructions
├── scripts/              # Helper scripts
│   └── process.sh
├── references/           # Detailed docs loaded on-demand
│   └── api-reference.md
└── assets/
    └── template.json
```

### SKILL.md Format

````markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: What this skill does and when to use it. Be specific.
---

# My Skill

## Setup

Run once before first use:
```bash
cd /path/to/skill && npm install
```

## Usage

```bash
./scripts/process.sh <input>
```
````

Use relative paths from the skill directory:

```markdown
See [the reference guide](references/REFERENCE.md) for details.
```

## Frontmatter

Per the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification#frontmatter-required):

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | Yes | Max 64 chars. Lowercase a-z, 0-9, hyphens. Unlike the standard, Pi does not require this to match the parent directory because that standard requirement is suboptimal for shared skill directories. |
| `description` | Yes | Max 1024 chars. What the skill does and when to use it. |
| `license` | No | License name or reference to bundled file. |
| `compatibility` | No | Max 500 chars. Environment requirements. |
| `metadata` | No | Arbitrary key-value mapping. |
| `allowed-tools` | No | Space-delimited list of pre-approved tools (experimental). |
| `disable-model-invocation` | No | When `true`, skill is hidden from system prompt. Users must use `/skill:name`. |

### Name Rules

- 1-64 characters
- Lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens only
- No leading/trailing hyphens
- No consecutive hyphens
Pi does not require the name to match the parent directory. The Agent Skills standard does, but that requirement is suboptimal for shared skill directories used by multiple tools.

Valid: `pdf-processing`, `data-analysis`, `code-review`
Invalid: `PDF-Processing`, `-pdf`, `pdf--processing`

### Description Best Practices

The description determines when the agent loads the skill. Be specific.

Good:
```yaml
description: Extracts text and tables from PDF files, fills PDF forms, and merges multiple PDFs. Use when working with PDF documents.
```

Poor:
```yaml
description: Helps with PDFs.
```

## Validation

Pi validates skills against the Agent Skills standard. Most issues produce warnings but still load the skill:

- Name exceeds 64 characters or contains invalid characters
- Name starts/ends with hyphen or has consecutive hyphens
- Description exceeds 1024 characters

Unknown frontmatter fields are ignored.

**Exception:** Skills with missing description are not loaded.

Name collisions (same name from different locations) warn and keep the first skill found.

## Example

```
brave-search/
├── SKILL.md
├── search.js
└── content.js
```

**SKILL.md:**
````markdown
---
name: brave-search
description: Web search and content extraction via Brave Search API. Use for searching documentation, facts, or any web content.
---

# Brave Search

## Setup

```bash
cd /path/to/brave-search && npm install
```

## Search

```bash
./search.js "query"              # Basic search
./search.js "query" --content    # Include page content
```

## Extract Page Content

```bash
./content.js https://example.com
```
````

## Skill Repositories

- [Anthropic Skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) - Document processing (docx, pdf, pptx, xlsx), web development
- [Pi Skills](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-skills) - Web search, browser automation, Google APIs, transcription

> New issues and PRs from new contributors are auto-closed by default. Maintainers review auto-closed issues daily. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md). --- Pi is a minimal terminal coding harness. Adapt pi to your workflows, not the other way around, without having to fork and modify pi internals. Extend it with TypeScript [Extensions](#extensions), [Skills](#skills), [Prompt Templates](#prompt-templates), and [Themes](#themes). Put your extensions, skills, prompt templates, and themes in [Pi Packages](#pi-packages) and share them with others via npm or git. Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub agents and plan mode. Instead, you can ask pi to build what you want or install a third party pi package that matches your workflow. Pi runs in four modes: interactive, print or JSON, RPC for process integration, and an SDK for embedding in your own apps. See [openclaw/openclaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) for a real-world SDK integration. ## Share your OSS coding agent sessions If you use pi for open source work, please share your coding agent sessions. Public OSS session data helps improve models, prompts, tools, and evaluations using real development workflows. For the full explanation, see [this post on X](https://x.com/badlogicgames/status/2037811643774652911). To publish sessions, use [`badlogic/pi-share-hf`](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf). Read its README.md for setup instructions. All you need is a Hugging Face account, the Hugging Face CLI, and `pi-share-hf`. You can also watch [this video](https://x.com/badlogicgames/status/2041151967695634619), where I show how I publish my `pi-mono` sessions. I regularly publish my own `pi-mono` work sessions here: - [badlogicgames/pi-mono on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/badlogicgames/pi-mono) ## Table of Contents - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Providers & Models](#providers--models) - [Interactive Mode](#interactive-mode) - [Editor](#editor) - [Commands](#commands) - [Keyboard Shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts) - [Message Queue](#message-queue) - [Sessions](#sessions) - [Branching](#branching) - [Compaction](#compaction) - [Settings](#settings) - [Context Files](#context-files) - [Customization](#customization) - [Prompt Templates](#prompt-templates) - [Skills](#skills) - [Extensions](#extensions) - [Themes](#themes) - [Pi Packages](#pi-packages) - [Programmatic Usage](#programmatic-usage) - [Philosophy](#philosophy) - [CLI Reference](#cli-reference) --- ## Quick Start ```bash npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent ``` Authenticate with an API key: ```bash export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... pi ``` Or use your existing subscription: ```bash pi /login # Then select provider ``` Then just talk to pi. By default, pi gives the model four tools: `read`, `write`, `edit`, and `bash`. The model uses these to fulfill your requests. Add capabilities via [skills](#skills), [prompt templates](#prompt-templates), [extensions](#extensions), or [pi packages](#pi-packages). **Platform notes:** [Windows](docs/windows.md) | [Termux (Android)](docs/termux.md) | [tmux](docs/tmux.md) | [Terminal setup](docs/terminal-setup.md) | [Shell aliases](docs/shell-aliases.md) --- ## Providers & Models For each built-in provider, pi maintains a list of tool-capable models, updated with every release. Authenticate via subscription (`/login`) or API key, then select any model from that provider via `/model` (or Ctrl+L). **Subscriptions:** - Anthropic Claude Pro/Max - OpenAI ChatGPT Plus/Pro (Codex) - GitHub Copilot **API keys:** - Anthropic - OpenAI - Azure OpenAI - DeepSeek - Google Gemini - Google Vertex - Amazon Bedrock - Mistral - Groq - Cerebras - Cloudflare AI Gateway - Cloudflare Workers AI - xAI - OpenRouter - Vercel AI Gateway - ZAI - OpenCode Zen - OpenCode Go - Hugging Face - Fireworks - Kimi For Coding - MiniMax - Xiaomi MiMo - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (China) - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (Amsterdam) - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (Singapore) See [docs/providers.md](docs/providers.md) for detailed setup instructions. **Custom providers & models:** Add providers via `~/.pi/agent/models.json` if they speak a supported API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google). For custom APIs or OAuth, use extensions. See [docs/models.md](docs/models.md) and [docs/custom-provider.md](docs/custom-provider.md). --- ## Interactive Mode

The interface from top to bottom: - **Startup header** - Shows shortcuts (`/hotkeys` for all), loaded AGENTS.md files, prompt templates, skills, and extensions - **Messages** - Your messages, assistant responses, tool calls and results, notifications, errors, and extension UI - **Editor** - Where you type; border color indicates thinking level - **Footer** - Working directory, session name, total token/cache usage, cost, context usage, current model The editor can be temporarily replaced by other UI, like built-in `/settings` or custom UI from extensions (e.g., a Q&A tool that lets the user answer model questions in a structured format). [Extensions](#extensions) can also replace the editor, add widgets above/below it, a status line, custom footer, or overlays. ### Editor | Feature | How | |---------|-----| | File reference | Type `@` to fuzzy-search project files | | Path completion | Tab to complete paths | | Multi-line | Shift+Enter (or Ctrl+Enter on Windows Terminal) | | Images | Ctrl+V to paste (Alt+V on Windows), or drag onto terminal | | Bash commands | `!command` runs and sends output to LLM, `!!command` runs without sending | Standard editing keybindings for delete word, undo, etc. See [docs/keybindings.md](docs/keybindings.md). ### Commands Type `/` in the editor to trigger commands. [Extensions](#extensions) can register custom commands, [skills](#skills) are available as `/skill:name`, and [prompt templates](#prompt-templates) expand via `/templatename`. | Command | Description | |---------|-------------| | `/login`, `/logout` | OAuth authentication | | `/model` | Switch models | | `/scoped-models` | Enable/disable models for Ctrl+P cycling | | `/settings` | Thinking level, theme, message delivery, transport | | `/resume` | Pick from previous sessions | | `/new` | Start a new session | | `/name ` | Set session display name | | `/session` | Show session info (file, ID, messages, tokens, cost) | | `/tree` | Jump to any point in the session and continue from there | | `/fork` | Create a new session from a previous user message | | `/clone` | Duplicate the current active branch into a new session | | `/compact [prompt]` | Manually compact context, optional custom instructions | | `/copy` | Copy last assistant message to clipboard | | `/export [file]` | Export session to HTML file | | `/share` | Upload as private GitHub gist with shareable HTML link | | `/reload` | Reload keybindings, extensions, skills, prompts, and context files (themes hot-reload automatically) | | `/hotkeys` | Show all keyboard shortcuts | | `/changelog` | Display version history | | `/quit` | Quit pi | ### Keyboard Shortcuts See `/hotkeys` for the full list. > New issues and PRs from new contributors are auto-closed by default. Maintainers review auto-closed issues daily. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md). --- Pi is a minimal terminal coding harness. Adapt pi to your workflows, not the other way around, without having to fork and modify pi internals. Extend it with TypeScript [Extensions](#extensions), [Skills](#skills), [Prompt Templates](#prompt-templates), and [Themes](#themes). Put your extensions, skills, prompt templates, and themes in [Pi Packages](#pi-packages) and share them with others via npm or git. Pi ships with powerful defaults but skips features like sub agents and plan mode. Instead, you can ask pi to build what you want or install a third party pi package that matches your workflow. Pi runs in four modes: interactive, print or JSON, RPC for process integration, and an SDK for embedding in your own apps. See [openclaw/openclaw](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) for a real-world SDK integration. ## Share your OSS coding agent sessions If you use pi for open source work, please share your coding agent sessions. Public OSS session data helps improve models, prompts, tools, and evaluations using real development workflows. For the full explanation, see [this post on X](https://x.com/badlogicgames/status/2037811643774652911). To publish sessions, use [`badlogic/pi-share-hf`](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf). Read its README.md for setup instructions. All you need is a Hugging Face account, the Hugging Face CLI, and `pi-share-hf`. You can also watch [this video](https://x.com/badlogicgames/status/2041151967695634619), where I show how I publish my `pi-mono` sessions. I regularly publish my own `pi-mono` work sessions here: - [badlogicgames/pi-mono on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/badlogicgames/pi-mono) ## Table of Contents - [Quick Start](#quick-start) - [Providers & Models](#providers--models) - [Interactive Mode](#interactive-mode) - [Editor](#editor) - [Commands](#commands) - [Keyboard Shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts) - [Message Queue](#message-queue) - [Sessions](#sessions) - [Branching](#branching) - [Compaction](#compaction) - [Settings](#settings) - [Context Files](#context-files) - [Customization](#customization) - [Prompt Templates](#prompt-templates) - [Skills](#skills) - [Extensions](#extensions) - [Themes](#themes) - [Pi Packages](#pi-packages) - [Programmatic Usage](#programmatic-usage) - [Philosophy](#philosophy) - [CLI Reference](#cli-reference) --- ## Quick Start ```bash npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent ``` Authenticate with an API key: ```bash export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... pi ``` Or use your existing subscription: ```bash pi /login # Then select provider ``` Then just talk to pi. By default, pi gives the model four tools: `read`, `write`, `edit`, and `bash`. The model uses these to fulfill your requests. Add capabilities via [skills](#skills), [prompt templates](#prompt-templates), [extensions](#extensions), or [pi packages](#pi-packages). **Platform notes:** [Windows](docs/windows.md) | [Termux (Android)](docs/termux.md) | [tmux](docs/tmux.md) | [Terminal setup](docs/terminal-setup.md) | [Shell aliases](docs/shell-aliases.md) --- ## Providers & Models For each built-in provider, pi maintains a list of tool-capable models, updated with every release. Authenticate via subscription (`/login`) or API key, then select any model from that provider via `/model` (or Ctrl+L). **Subscriptions:** - Anthropic Claude Pro/Max - OpenAI ChatGPT Plus/Pro (Codex) - GitHub Copilot **API keys:** - Anthropic - OpenAI - Azure OpenAI - DeepSeek - Google Gemini - Google Vertex - Amazon Bedrock - Mistral - Groq - Cerebras - Cloudflare AI Gateway - Cloudflare Workers AI - xAI - OpenRouter - Vercel AI Gateway - ZAI - OpenCode Zen - OpenCode Go - Hugging Face - Fireworks - Kimi For Coding - MiniMax - Xiaomi MiMo - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (China) - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (Amsterdam) - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan (Singapore) See [docs/providers.md](docs/providers.md) for detailed setup instructions. **Custom providers & models:** Add providers via `~/.pi/agent/models.json` if they speak a supported API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google). For custom APIs or OAuth, use extensions. See [docs/models.md](docs/models.md) and [docs/custom-provider.md](docs/custom-provider.md). --- ## Interactive Mode

The interface from top to bottom: - **Startup header** - Shows shortcuts (`/hotkeys` for all), loaded AGENTS.md files, prompt templates, skills, and extensions - **Messages** - Your messages, assistant responses, tool calls and results, notifications, errors, and extension UI - **Editor** - Where you type; border color indicates thinking level - **Footer** - Working directory, session name, total token/cache usage, cost, context usage, current model The editor can be temporarily replaced by other UI, like built-in `/settings` or custom UI from extensions (e.g., a Q&A tool that lets the user answer model questions in a structured format). [Extensions](#extensions) can also replace the editor, add widgets above/below it, a status line, custom footer, or overlays. ### Editor | Feature | How | |---------|-----| | File reference | Type `@` to fuzzy-search project files | | Path completion | Tab to complete paths | | Multi-line | Shift+Enter (or Ctrl+Enter on Windows Terminal) | | Images | Ctrl+V to paste (Alt+V on Windows), or drag onto terminal | | Bash commands | `!command` runs and sends output to LLM, `!!command` runs without sending | Standard editing keybindings for delete word, undo, etc. See [docs/keybindings.md](docs/keybindings.md). ### Commands Type `/` in the editor to trigger commands. [Extensions](#extensions) can register custom commands, [skills](#skills) are available as `/skill:name`, and [prompt templates](#prompt-templates) expand via `/templatename`. | Command | Description | |---------|-------------| | `/login`, `/logout` | OAuth authentication | | `/model` | Switch models | | `/scoped-models` | Enable/disable models for Ctrl+P cycling | | `/settings` | Thinking level, theme, message delivery, transport | | `/resume` | Pick from previous sessions | | `/new` | Start a new session | | `/name ` | Set session display name | | `/session` | Show session info (file, ID, messages, tokens, cost) | | `/tree` | Jump to any point in the session and continue from there | | `/fork` | Create a new session from a previous user message | | `/clone` | Duplicate the current active branch into a new session | | `/compact [prompt]` | Manually compact context, optional custom instructions | | `/copy` | Copy last assistant message to clipboard | | `/export [file]` | Export session to HTML file | | `/share` | Upload as private GitHub gist with shareable HTML link | | `/reload` | Reload keybindings, extensions, skills, prompts, and context files (themes hot-reload automatically) | | `/hotkeys` | Show all keyboard shortcuts | | `/changelog` | Display version history | | `/quit` | Quit pi | ### Keyboard Shortcuts See `/hotkeys` for the full list. ---
name: "dev:trigger-analysis"
description: "Trigger checkpoint analysis generation for checkpoints via the local dev API"
---

Trigger checkpoint analysis generation for one or more checkpoints using the local dev API endpoint.

Parse `$ARGUMENTS` using natural language to determine the mode:

## Mode A: Explicit checkpoint IDs with repo

If `$ARGUMENTS` contains a repo name (contains a `/`) and one or more checkpoint ID strings, use them directly.

Example: `/dev:trigger-analysis entirehq/entire.io abc123 def456`

Run:

```
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8787/api/v1/dev/analysis \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"repo": "<repo>", "checkpoint_ids": ["<id1>", "<id2>", "..."]}'
```

## Mode B: Explicit checkpoint IDs without repo

If `$ARGUMENTS` contains checkpoint IDs but no repo name, look up the repo from the local database first:

```
mysql -u entire -pentire -h 127.0.0.1 entire -N -e \
  "SELECT r.full_name FROM repos r JOIN repo_checkpoints rc ON r.id = rc.repo_id WHERE rc.checkpoint_id = '<first_id>' LIMIT 1"
```

Then use Mode A with the discovered repo name.

## Mode C: Most recent N checkpoints for a repo

If `$ARGUMENTS` contains a number and a repo name (contains a `/`), query the local MySQL database for the most recent checkpoint IDs.

Example: `/dev:trigger-analysis 3 entirehq/entire.io`

First, query for checkpoint IDs ordered by `created_at`:

```
mysql -u entire -pentire -h 127.0.0.1 entire -N -e \
  "SELECT checkpoint_id FROM repo_checkpoints WHERE repo_id = (SELECT id FROM repos WHERE full_name = '<repo>') ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT <N>"
```

Then use the resulting checkpoint IDs with Mode A.

## After the curl completes

1. If the response is valid JSON, display it formatted nicely with key fields highlighted.
2. If the connection is refused (exit code 7 or "Connection refused" in output), tell the user: "The local API server is not running. Start it with `mise run api`."
3. If the response contains an error field, display the error message clearly.

## If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty

Ask the user to provide either:

- one or more checkpoint IDs, or
- a number and repo name (for example `3 entirehq/entire.io`)

    68	3. When a task matches, the agent uses `read` to load the full SKILL.md (models don't always do this; use prompting or `/skill:name` to force it)
    69	4. The agent follows the instructions, using relative paths to reference scripts and assets
    70	
    71	This is progressive disclosure: only descriptions are always in context, full instructions load on-demand.
    72	
    73	## Skill Commands
    74	
    75	Skills register as `/skill:name` commands:
    76	
    77	```bash
    78	/skill:brave-search           # Load and execute the skill
    79	/skill:pdf-tools extract      # Load skill with arguments
    80	```
    81	
    82	Arguments after the command are appended to the skill content as `User: <args>`.
    83	
    84	Toggle skill commands via `/settings` in interactive mode or in `settings.json`:
    85	
    86	```json
    87	{
    88	  "enableSkillCommands": true
    89	}
    90	```

content.text:
Investigated. Short answer: **not reliably from agent logs/transcripts across all agents today**. We can do **high-confidence, agent-specific detection** in some cases, but “Skill used” is not a uniform event.

Findings:

- **Raw `.entire/logs/entire.log` lifecycle logs** only have session/turn/checkpoint events + `session_ref`. They do **not** contain skill invocation data.
- **Current API analysis** derives `skillsUsed` only from parsed `toolCalls`:
  - `api/src/lib/analysis-queue.ts` calls `parser.extractSkillFromTool`.
  - Only **Claude Code** currently implements this reliably: `ToolCall.name === "Skill"` and `input.skill`.
  - **Codex explicitly returns null** (`Codex has no Skill-tool equivalent`).
  - Gemini/Amp/etc return null or don’t expose enough.
  - Pi parser currently does not extract skills.
- **False-positive traps**:
  - Codex logs include `<skills_instructions>` listing available skills. That is availability, not usage; our parser treats it as synthetic wrapper text.
  - Skill docs/content can appear in transcripts (`Base directory for this skill:`, `/skills/...`, `SKILL.md`) when injected or read. That may indicate context loading, not necessarily a skill being intentionally used.
- **Pi** is different:
  - Auto skill use means the model reads a `SKILL.md`.
  - `/skill:name` expands into a user message like `<skill name="..." location="...">...`.
  - Neither path is represented as a `Skill` tool call, so current metrics miss it.
- **CLI `entire review` has a better signal**:
  - It already records configured review skills via `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS` → `state.ReviewSkills` → checkpoint `review_skills`.
  - That is reliable for “we launched this review with these skills,” but not proof that every agent’s native skill mechanism fired. Example: Codex `/review` is expanded into plain prompt text.

Conclusion:

- **Reliable:** Claude Code `Skill` tool events; `entire review` configured `review_skills`.
- **Best-effort only:** inferring from `SKILL.md` reads, injected skill content, slash commands, or prompt text.
- **Not reliable cross-agent:** a single parser over logs/transcripts cannot prove skill usage for all agents.

Recommendation: add a normalized structured event at capture time, e.g. `skill_invocation {agent, session_id, skill_name, trigger_type, source_path, timestamp}`. For historical backfill, use confidence levels: `explicit_tool`, `review_metadata`, `slash_expansion`, `skill_file_read`, `prompt_heuristic`.
So, tl;dr we could do it as part of the CLI?

content.text:
Yes — **that’s the right place to do it**, with one caveat:

**Do it in the CLI as structured metadata, not by later parsing logs.**

Practical version:

- For `entire review`: we basically already can. CLI records configured skills via `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS` / `ReviewSkills` / checkpoint metadata.
- For normal sessions: add a normalized `skills_used` / `skill_invocations` field to session/checkpoint metadata.
- Populate it in agent-specific CLI adapters:
  - Claude Code: explicit `Skill` tool call → reliable.
  - Pi: detect `/skill:name` expansion or `<skill name="...">` injected block → reliable if captured by Pi/CLI integration.
  - Codex/Gemini: only reliable when CLI itself launched/configured the skill; native auto-skill usage is not reliably inferable today.

So TL;DR:

**Yes for future data if the CLI records it at runtime.**  
**No, not reliably for historical data by transcript/log parsing alone.**

/** V1 session metadata (CommittedMetadata) - stored per-session */
export interface CommittedMetadata {
  checkpoint_id: string
  session_id: string
  strategy: string
  created_at: string
  branch?: string
  checkpoints_count: number
  files_touched: string[]
  agent: string
  is_task?: boolean
  tool_use_id?: string
  transcript_identifier_at_start?: string
  /** @deprecated Use checkpoint_transcript_start instead */
  transcript_lines_at_start?: number
  checkpoint_transcript_start?: number
  model?: string
  token_usage?: TokenUsage
  summary?: SessionSummary
  initial_attribution?: InitialAttribution
}

/** Session summary from AI analysis */
export interface SessionSummary {
  intent: string
  outcome: string
  learnings: {
    repo: string[]
    code: Array<{ path: string; line: number; finding: string }>
    workflow: string[]
  }
  friction: string[]
  open_items: string[]
}

/** Attribution metrics calculated at checkpoint time */
export interface InitialAttribution {
  calculated_at: string
  agent_lines: number
  human_added: number
  human_modified: number
  human_removed: number
  total_committed: number
  agent_percentage: number
}

// Per-file stats for a commit
export interface FileStats {
  filename: string
  previousFilename?: string | null
  status: "added" | "removed" | "modified" | "renamed" | "copied" | "changed" | "unchanged"
  additions: number
  deletions: number
  patch?: string | null // Unified diff for this file
  patchTruncated?: boolean // True if patch was truncated due to size limits
}

export interface CheckpointInfo {
  // The commit on the branch (may be null if branch push webhook hasn't arrived yet)
  commitSha: string | null
  commitMessage: string | null
  commitSubject: string | null
  commitBody: string | null
  commitAuthor: string | null
  commitAuthorUsername: string | null
  commitDate: string | null
  // Diff stats from commit (may be null)
  additions: number | null
  deletions: number | null
  filesChanged: number | null
  filesTouched: string[] | null
  // Per-file stats with additions/deletions breakdown
  fileStats: FileStats[] | null
  // The checkpoint ID from Entire-Checkpoint trailer (maps to folder in session branch)
  checkpointId: string
  // Created at timestamp (from metadata.json, used for sorting when no commit date)
  createdAt: string
  // Sessions associated with this checkpoint
  sessions: SessionInfo[]
  // Number of sessions associated with this checkpoint
  sessionCount: number
  // Total steps across all sessions
  totalSteps: number
  // Unique agents involved in this checkpoint
  agents: string[]
  // Token usage (may be null if not tracked)
  inputTokens: number | null
  cacheCreationTokens: number | null
  cacheReadTokens: number | null
  outputTokens: number | null
  apiCallCount: number | null
  // Attribution metrics (may be null if not calculated)
  attribution: {
    calculatedAt: string
    agentLines: number
    humanAdded: number
    humanModified: number
    humanRemoved: number
    totalCommitted: number
    agentPercentage: number
  } | null
  // Repo where checkpoint data lives (differs from source repo for checkpoint_remote configs)
  checkpointRepoFullName: string | null
}

/**

content.text:
Yes. In `../cli`, I’d do it as an additive metadata pipeline:

### 1. Add a normalized type in CLI

New file, e.g. `cmd/entire/cli/agent/skills.go`:

```go
type SkillInvocation struct {
	Name       string `json:"name"`
	Invocation string `json:"invocation,omitempty"` // e.g. "/review"
	Source     string `json:"source"`               // claude_skill_tool, pi_skill_block, entire_review_config
	Confidence string `json:"confidence"`           // explicit, loaded, declared, inferred
	ToolUseID  string `json:"tool_use_id,omitempty"`
	SourcePath string `json:"source_path,omitempty"`
	Timestamp  string `json:"timestamp,omitempty"`
}

type SkillInvocationExtractor interface {
	Agent
	ExtractSkillInvocations(transcriptData []byte, fromOffset int) ([]SkillInvocation, error)
}
```

Add helper like `agent.CalculateTokenUsage(...)`:

```go
func ExtractSkillInvocations(ctx context.Context, ag Agent, data []byte, offset int) []SkillInvocation {
	if ex, ok := ag.(SkillInvocationExtractor); ok {
		out, err := ex.ExtractSkillInvocations(data, offset)
		if err != nil {
			// debug log and return nil
			return nil
		}
		return out
	}
	return nil
}
```

### 2. Persist it in checkpoint metadata

Add fields alongside existing `ReviewSkills`:

- `cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go`
- `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/checkpoint.go`
- `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_types.go`

Example:

```go
SkillInvocations []agent.SkillInvocation `json:"skill_invocations,omitempty"`
SkillsUsed       []string                `json:"skills_used,omitempty"`
```

`skills_used` is the denormalized unique list for easy API/facet ingestion. `skill_invocations` keeps provenance.

### 3. Populate during condensation

In `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go`, inside both transcript extraction paths:

```go
data.SkillInvocations = agent.ExtractSkillInvocations(
	ctx,
	ag,
	data.Transcript,
	checkpointTranscriptStart,
)
```

Then pass into `checkpoint.WriteCommittedOptions`:

```go
SkillInvocations: mergeSkillInvocations(state.SkillInvocations, sessionData.SkillInvocations),
SkillsUsed: uniqueSkillNames(...),
```

### 4. Keep current `entire review` signal

This already exists:

- `cmd/entire/cli/review/env.go`
- `cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go`
- `ReviewSkills []string`

In `adoptReviewEnv`, also convert `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS` into `SkillInvocation`s:

```go
for _, s := range skills {
	state.SkillInvocations = append(state.SkillInvocations, agent.SkillInvocation{
		Name:       normalizeSkillName(s),
		Invocation: s,
		Source:     "entire_review_config",
		Confidence: "declared",
	})
}
```

This is “configured/declared”, not proof the agent natively invoked it.

### 5. Implement per-agent extractors

Start with reliable ones:

#### Claude Code

In `cmd/entire/cli/agent/claudecode/transcript.go`:

- Parse assistant `tool_use` blocks.
- If `block.Name == "Skill"`, read `input.skill`.

That’s explicit and reliable.

#### Pi

In `cmd/entire/cli/agent/pi/transcript.go`:

Detect:

1. `/skill:name` expansion:
   - user content contains `<skill name="...">`
   - source: `pi_skill_block`
   - confidence: `explicit`

2. automatic progressive disclosure:
   - assistant `read` tool reads a `SKILL.md`
   - parse skill name from result frontmatter or path
   - source: `skill_file_read`
   - confidence: `loaded`

#### Codex / Gemini

Initially only use `entire_review_config`, because native skill activation is not reliably represented as a tool event.

### 6. Tests to add

- Claude: `Skill` tool call becomes `SkillInvocation`.
- Pi: `<skill name="x">` and `read .../SKILL.md` become invocations.
- Review lifecycle: `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS` populates `skill_invocations`.
- Checkpoint metadata JSON includes both `review_skills` and `skill_invocations`.

### TL;DR implementation path

Do this in CLI metadata, not logs:

```txt
agent transcript / review config
        ↓
agent.SkillInvocationExtractor
        ↓
session/checkpoint metadata.json
        ↓
API hydrator ingests skills_used / skill_invocations
        ↓
analysis facets
```

I’d implement Claude + `entire review` first, then Pi next.

## Goal
Determine whether agent logs/transcripts can reliably identify when Skills are used, and whether this should be implemented in the CLI.

## Constraints & Preferences
- Skills are triggered differently per agent.
- Prefer reliable structured runtime metadata over heuristic log parsing.

## Progress
### Done
- [x] Investigated `.entire/logs/entire.log`, API transcript parsers, Pi docs/source, and CLI review metadata flow.
- [x] Found API currently derives `skillsUsed` via `extractToolMetricsFromSessions` in `api/src/lib/analysis-queue.ts`, calling `parser.extractSkillFromTool`.
- [x] Confirmed Claude Code has the reliable signal: explicit `Skill` tool calls with `input.skill`.
- [x] Confirmed Codex/Gemini/Pi do not expose a uniform reliable Skill event in transcripts today.
- [x] Identified CLI review metadata path: `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS` → `state.ReviewSkills` → checkpoint `review_skills`.

### In Progress
- [ ] No implementation started yet.

### Blocked
- Historical cross-agent detection is blocked by lack of uniform Skill events in raw logs/transcripts.

## Key Decisions
- **Implement in CLI, not post-hoc log parsing**: CLI can emit normalized structured metadata at runtime; transcript heuristics are unreliable.
- **Treat historical parsing as confidence-based only**: Signals like `SKILL.md`, `/skills/...`, `<skills_instructions>`, or `Base directory for this skill:` are not definitive proof of usage.

## Next Steps
1. Add normalized CLI metadata such as `skill_invocations` or `skills_used`.

content.text:
Correct — the checkpoint stores the agent’s raw transcript/logs, redacted/chunked, not a rewritten normalized transcript.

But the CLI still has a metadata write step.

Flow is roughly:

```txt
agent runs
  ↓
CLI hooks copy/read raw agent transcript
  ↓
SaveStep writes temporary shadow checkpoint
  ↓
git post-commit triggers CondenseSession
  ↓
CLI writes:
  - raw/redacted transcript
  - prompt.txt
  - metadata.json
```

So “condense” here does **not** mean summarizing or transforming the transcript. It means “take the raw agent transcript and checkpoint state, then persist it into Entire checkpoint storage with metadata.”

That means the better implementation is:

- leave raw transcript untouched
- add normalized skill fields to `metadata.json`

Something like:

```json
{
  "review_skills": ["trigger-analysis"],
  "skills_used": ["trigger-analysis"],
  "skill_invocations": [
    {
      "name": "trigger-analysis",
      "source": "claude_skill_tool",
      "confidence": "explicit",
      "tool_use_id": "toolu_..."
    }
  ]
}
```

The subtle part: because the CLI does **not** condense immediately on every tool call, there are two implementation options:

### Option A — extract at condensation time

When `CondenseSession` reads the raw transcript, also extract skill invocations from the checkpoint-scoped transcript region.

This is easiest and works for Claude because the raw transcript contains explicit `Skill` tool calls.

### Option B — record at runtime, persist later

For stronger correctness, especially cross-agent, add runtime events/state:

- Claude: install a `PostToolUse` hook for matcher `Skill`
- parse `tool_input.skill`
- append to `SessionState.SkillInvocations`
- later `CondenseSession` persists that into checkpoint metadata

This avoids relying on historical/raw transcript parsing where hooks provide an explicit event.

So yes: the stored transcript is raw agent logs. The proposed CLI change should be a **sidecar metadata addition**, not a transcript rewrite.
So, how can we determine the skill invokation or prompt later? Because that's the whole point. To be able to identifiy which prompt was a skill instead of just user message.

Today, from only `prompt.txt` or raw transcript, we generally **cannot reliably tell**. Once a skill expansion is written as ordinary text in the transcript, it can be indistinguishable from the user pasting that same text.

So the CLI change needs to store **prompt provenance**, not just `skills_used`.

Add metadata like this:

```json
{
  "prompt_events": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "turn_id": "turn_abc",
      "kind": "user",
      "transcript_start": 120,
      "transcript_end": 143
    },
    {
      "index": 1,
      "turn_id": "turn_def",
      "kind": "skill_command",
      "skill": "trigger-analysis",
      "invocation": "/skill:trigger-analysis",
      "transcript_start": 144,
      "transcript_end": 160
    }
  ],
  "skill_invocations": [
    {
      "name": "trigger-analysis",
      "source": "claude_skill_tool",
      "confidence": "explicit",
      "turn_id": "turn_def",
      "prompt_index": 1,
      "tool_use_id": "toolu_..."
    }
  ]
}
```

Then later the API/UI does **not infer** from raw transcript. It reads metadata and can say:

- prompt 0 was a normal user prompt
- prompt 1 was a skill command / generated skill prompt
- turn `turn_def` invoked skill `trigger-analysis`

Agent-specific behavior:

- **Claude Code**: skill is usually not a user prompt. It is an explicit assistant tool call: `Skill` with `input.skill`. Store that as `skill_invocations`, linked to the current `turn_id` / nearest prompt.
- **Pi**: if `/skill:name` expands into a prompt, record that expansion as `prompt_events.kind = "skill_command"` or `"skill_expansion"` at runtime. If we only see `<skill name="...">` later in the raw transcript, that’s heuristic.
- **`entire review`**: CLI already knows the generated review prompt and configured skills. Store the prompt as `kind = "review_prompt"` and link declared skills.
- **Codex/Gemini**: unless the CLI launched/configured the skill, treat as unknown. Don’t guess.

So the key correction is:

> `skills_used` alone answers “which skills were involved”; it does not answer “which prompt was a skill.”  
> For that, add `prompt_events` / prompt provenance metadata with transcript anchors and skill links.
We technically only need to mark or "store" the initial event in the metadata json?

Yes — if the goal is “later know this prompt came from a skill”, then you only need to persist a small **provenance marker** in checkpoint metadata.

You do **not** need to rewrite the raw transcript.

But don’t store only `skills_used`; store an event/annotation with enough anchors to map back to the prompt:

```json
{
  "prompt_events": [
    {
      "turn_id": "turn_abc",
      "prompt_index": 0,
      "kind": "skill",
      "skill": "trigger-analysis",
      "invocation": "/skill:trigger-analysis",
      "source": "pi_slash_skill",
      "confidence": "explicit",
      "transcript_start": 120,
      "prompt_sha256": "..."
    }
  ]
}
```

Minimal fields I’d keep:

```txt
turn_id
prompt_index or transcript_start
kind: user | skill | review_prompt
skill
invocation
source
confidence
optional prompt hash
```

Important nuance: checkpoint `metadata.json` doesn’t exist until condensation/post-commit, so at runtime the CLI should first store this in session state, e.g.

```txt
.git/entire-sessions/<session>.json
```

Then when `CondenseSession` writes committed metadata, copy it into:

```txt
<checkpoint>/N/metadata.json
```

Later API/UI flow becomes:

```txt
read prompt.txt / transcript
read metadata.prompt_events
join by prompt_index / turn_id / transcript_start
display: “this prompt was skill trigger-analysis”
```

For `entire review`, this is very straightforward because CLI already knows the generated prompt and configured skills.

For Claude Code, if the signal is a `Skill` tool call rather than a slash prompt, store that as `skill_invocations` linked to the active `turn_id`; it may not mean the original user prompt itself was a skill prompt.

content.text:
> pi can create skills. Ask it to build one for your use case.

# Skills

Skills are self-contained capability packages that the agent loads on-demand. A skill provides specialized workflows, setup instructions, helper scripts, and reference documentation for specific tasks.

Pi implements the [Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io/specification), warning about most violations but remaining lenient. Pi allows skill names to differ from their parent directory even though the standard disallows it; that rule is suboptimal for shared skill directories used across multiple agent harnesses.

## Table of Contents

- [Locations](#locations)
- [How Skills Work](#how-skills-work)
- [Skill Commands](#skill-commands)
- [Skill Structure](#skill-structure)
- [Frontmatter](#frontmatter)
- [Validation](#validation)
- [Example](#example)
- [Skill Repositories](#skill-repositories)

## Locations

> **Security:** Skills can instruct the model to perform any action and may include executable code the model invokes. Review skill content before use.

Pi loads skills from:

- Global:
  - `~/.pi/agent/skills/`
  - `~/.agents/skills/`
- Project:
  - `.pi/skills/`
  - `.agents/skills/` in `cwd` and ancestor directories (up to git repo root, or filesystem root when not in a repo)
- Packages: `skills/` directories or `pi.skills` entries in `package.json`
- Settings: `skills` array with files or directories
- CLI: `--skill <path>` (repeatable, additive even with `--no-skills`)

Discovery rules:
- In `~/.pi/agent/skills/` and `.pi/skills/`, direct root `.md` files are discovered as individual skills
- In all skill locations, directories containing `SKILL.md` are discovered recursively
- In `~/.agents/skills/` and project `.agents/skills/`, root `.md` files are ignored

Disable discovery with `--no-skills` (explicit `--skill` paths still load).

### Using Skills from Other Harnesses

To use skills from Claude Code or OpenAI Codex, add their directories to settings:

```json
{
  "skills": [
    "~/.claude/skills",
    "~/.codex/skills"
  ]
}
```

For project-level Claude Code skills, add to `.pi/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "skills": ["../.claude/skills"]
}
```

## How Skills Work

1. At startup, pi scans skill locations and extracts names and descriptions
2. The system prompt includes available skills in XML format per the [specification](https://agentskills.io/integrate-skills)
3. When a task matches, the agent uses `read` to load the full SKILL.md (models don't always do this; use prompting or `/skill:name` to force it)
4. The agent follows the instructions, using relative paths to reference scripts and assets

This is progressive disclosure: only descriptions are always in context, full instructions load on-demand.

## Skill Commands

Skills register as `/skill:name` commands:

```bash
/skill:brave-search           # Load and execute the skill
/skill:pdf-tools extract      # Load skill with arguments
```

Arguments after the command are appended to the skill content as `User: <args>`.

Toggle skill commands via `/settings` in interactive mode or in `settings.json`:

```json
{
  "enableSkillCommands": true
}
```

## Skill Structure

A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md` file. Everything else is freeform.

```
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md              # Required: frontmatter + instructions
├── scripts/              # Helper scripts
│   └── process.sh
├── references/           # Detailed docs loaded on-demand
│   └── api-reference.md
└── assets/
    └── template.json
```

### SKILL.md Format

````markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: What this skill does and when to use it. Be specific.
---

# My Skill

## Setup

Run once before first use:
```bash
cd /path/to/skill && npm install
```

## Usage

```bash
./scripts/process.sh <input>
```
````

Use relative paths from the skill directory:

```markdown
See [the reference guide](references/REFERENCE.md) for details.
```

## Frontmatter

Per the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification#frontmatter-required):

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | Yes | Max 64 chars. Lowercase a-z, 0-9, hyphens. Unlike the standard, Pi does not require this to match the parent directory because that standard requirement is suboptimal for shared skill directories. |
| `description` | Yes | Max 1024 chars. What the skill does and when to use it. |
| `license` | No | License name or reference to bundled file. |
| `compatibility` | No | Max 500 chars. Environment requirements. |
| `metadata` | No | Arbitrary key-value mapping. |
| `allowed-tools` | No | Space-delimited list of pre-approved tools (experimental). |
| `disable-model-invocation` | No | When `true`, skill is hidden from system prompt. Users must use `/skill:name`. |

### Name Rules

- 1-64 characters
- Lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens only
- No leading/trailing hyphens
- No consecutive hyphens
Pi does not require the name to match the parent directory. The Agent Skills standard does, but that requirement is suboptimal for shared skill directories used by multiple tools.

Valid: `pdf-processing`, `data-analysis`, `code-review`
Invalid: `PDF-Processing`, `-pdf`, `pdf--processing`

### Description Best Practices

The description determines when the agent loads the skill. Be specific.

Good:
```yaml
description: Extracts text and tables from PDF files, fills PDF forms, and merges multiple PDFs. Use when working with PDF documents.
```

Poor:
```yaml
description: Helps with PDFs.
```

## Validation

Pi validates skills against the Agent Skills standard. Most issues produce warnings but still load the skill:

- Name exceeds 64 characters or contains invalid characters
- Name starts/ends with hyphen or has consecutive hyphens
- Description exceeds 1024 characters

Unknown frontmatter fields are ignored.

**Exception:** Skills with missing description are not loaded.

Name collisions (same name from different locations) warn and keep the first skill found.

## Example

```
brave-search/
├── SKILL.md
├── search.js
└── content.js
```

**SKILL.md:**
````markdown
---
name: brave-search
description: Web search and content extraction via Brave Search API. Use for searching documentation, facts, or any web content.
---

# Brave Search

## Setup

```bash
cd /path/to/brave-search && npm install
```

## Search

```bash
./search.js "query"              # Basic search
./search.js "query" --content    # Include page content
```

## Extract Page Content

```bash
./content.js https://example.com
```
````

## Skill Repositories

- [Anthropic Skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) - Document processing (docx, pdf, pptx, xlsx), web development
- [Pi Skills](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-skills) - Web search, browser automation, Google APIs, transcription

**Determining agent signals**

I need to build an answer focused on how to determine signals for agents. The question is about deciding what metadata to use for marking initial events. I should include a table to clarify my response. 

For direct CLI-originated runs, it’s independent and can record `prompt_event` at TurnStart since CLI manages the entire prompt. The generated prompt content is already known, which helps identify skills or reviews. 

For interactive user-entered skills, I need to check if the agent has a pre-turn hook to parse raw prompts before they are expanded.

**Storing `prompt_origin`**

I need to ensure I store the `prompt_origin`. If an agent doesn’t provide a raw prompt hook or command syntax, I won’t be able to reliably determine the origin, relying only on post-hoc heuristics. 

For model-invoked skills, if the agent emits a tool call or extension event, I can capture that as `skill_invocation`, linking it to the current turn, but not to the prompt type. 

Specifically for Claude, the `UserPromptSubmit` hook shows the prompt in the lifecycle. I’ll detect if it includes a slash and track relevant skill tool use during the same turn.

**Handling skill commands in Pi**

For Pi, the `before_agent_start` hook carries the raw `prompt` from the extension. If the prompt begins with `/skill:<name>`, I should classify it as a skill command and store it in the session state before expanding.

Additionally, the transcript can include `<skill name="...">` or readings from SKILL.md, which I can use as a secondary source with lower confidence, mapping via transcript offsets.

Pi also has a `tool_call` extension event, but since it currently modifies bash, I could consider adding a handler to capture reads of SKILL.md as well.

content.text:
Per agent, use the **earliest structured signal** the agent gives us. If none exists, don’t guess.

| Agent | How to determine it | What to store |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Reliable skill use is assistant tool call: `tool_use.name == "Skill"` and `input.skill`. This is not necessarily a user prompt; it is a model-invoked skill inside the current turn. | `skill_invocations[]` linked to `turn_id` / prompt offset. |
| **Pi** | Reliable skill prompt is raw prompt beginning with `/skill:name`, from Pi’s `before_agent_start` hook. Pi may also later show `<skill name="...">` or read `SKILL.md`, but those are secondary signals. | `prompt_events[]` with `kind: "skill"`, `skill: name`, `invocation: "/skill:name"`. |
| **Codex** | No reliable native skill invocation event today. But Codex `UserPromptSubmit` hook gives raw prompt, so only classify if CLI itself supplied/recognized the skill command, e.g. `entire review` skills. | `prompt_events[]` from CLI-known prompt/config only. |
| **Gemini CLI** | Same: hook gives prompt, but no uniform native skill event. Use only CLI-known/configured skills or explicit recognized prompt syntax. | `prompt_events[]` from CLI-known prompt/config only. |
| **Cursor / OpenCode / Copilot / Droid** | Same pattern: if TurnStart hook includes raw prompt, classify explicit command syntax. If no native skill event, no reliable detection. | Prompt provenance only when explicit/CLI-known. |
| **entire review** | Agent-independent. CLI composes the prompt and already has `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SKILLS`. | `prompt_events.kind = "review_prompt"` plus declared skills. |

The important distinction:

```txt
prompt provenance  = "this prompt was generated from /skill:x"
skill invocation   = "the model loaded/used skill x during this turn"
```

For example:

### Pi `/skill:x`

```json
{
  "prompt_events": [
    {
      "turn_id": "turn_123",
      "kind": "skill",
      "skill": "trigger-analysis",
      "invocation": "/skill:trigger-analysis",
      "source": "pi_before_agent_start",
      "confidence": "explicit",
      "transcript_start": 120
    }
  ]
}
```

### Claude Code Skill tool

```json
{
  "prompt_events": [
    {
      "turn_id": "turn_123",
      "kind": "user",
      "transcript_start": 120
    }
  ],
  "skill_invocations": [
    {
      "turn_id": "turn_123",
      "name": "trigger-analysis",
      "source": "claude_skill_tool",
      "confidence": "explicit",
      "tool_use_id": "toolu_..."
    }
  ]
}
```

So the implementation should be:

1. At `TurnStart`, classify the raw prompt per agent.
2. Store that in session state.
3. If the agent exposes explicit skill tool events, append those too.
4. At condensation, copy staged events into checkpoint `metadata.json`.

Later, the API does not parse raw transcript heuristically; it reads `prompt_events` / `skill_invocations` from metadata.
Ignore entire review. The goal is to know which events were skills and potentially collapse them, no more.

### Per-agent determination

| Agent | Reliable signal | Collapse target |
|---|---|---|
| **Pi** | Add `pi.on("input")`; it sees raw input before `/skill:name` expansion. If raw input starts `/skill:foo`, mark next prompt event as skill. | Collapse the user/prompt event. |

| **Gemini CLI** | Same: `BeforeAgent` prompt can be checked for explicit skill syntax, but no native reliable skill event. | Collapse prompt only when explicit. |
| **Cursor / OpenCode / Copilot / Droid** | Same rule: if TurnStart/UserPrompt hook exposes raw prompt and it matches an explicit skill invocation. Otherwise unknown. | Collapse prompt only when explicit. |

Do **not** treat these as reliable:

```txt
read SKILL.md
path contains /skills/
prompt contains skill instructions
<skill name="..."> in expanded content
```

Those can be useful heuristics, but not enough to decide “this event was a skill” for collapsing.

So the implementation should be:

1. Add `skill_events` to session state.
2. At agent hook/runtime parsing, append explicit skill events.
3. At condensation, copy `skill_events` into checkpoint `metadata.json`.
4. UI/API collapses only events referenced by `skill_events`.

Plan: only mark **explicit skill signals**. If an agent doesn’t expose one, emit no `skill_events` and don’t collapse.

## Metadata target

Per session `metadata.json`:

```json
{
  "skill_events_version": 1,
  "skill_events": [
    {
      "id": "sk_evt_...",
      "event_type": "prompt_invocation",
      "skill": { "name": "trigger-analysis" },
      "source": {
        "agent": "pi",
        "signal": "input_slash_command"
      },
      "turn_id": "turn_abc",
      "transcript_anchor": {
        "unit": "line",
        "start": 84,
        "end": 85,
        "entry_ids": ["msg_123"]
      },
      "native": {
        "command": "/skill:trigger-analysis"
      },
      "collapse": {
        "target": "user_message",
        "label": "/skill:trigger-analysis",
        "default_collapsed": true
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Per-agent plan

| Agent | Reliable signal | How to capture | Collapse target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pi** | Raw `/skill:name` before expansion | Add `pi.on("input")` in the Pi extension. It sees raw input before Pi expands the skill. If it starts `/skill:name`, stash/emit a skill event for the next `before_agent_start`. | The resulting user prompt / expanded skill prompt. |
| **Claude Code** | `Skill` tool call with `input.skill` | Parse transcript assistant `tool_use` blocks where `name == "Skill"`, or install `PostToolUse` matcher for `Skill` and record at runtime. | The `Skill` tool call + corresponding tool result. |
| **Codex** | None currently, unless raw prompt has a verified skill command syntax | Use `UserPromptSubmit` raw prompt only if Codex has a confirmed explicit skill syntax. Otherwise emit nothing. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **Gemini CLI** | None currently, unless raw prompt has a verified skill command syntax | Use `BeforeAgent` prompt only if Gemini has a confirmed explicit skill syntax. Otherwise emit nothing. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **Cursor** | None currently, unless raw prompt has explicit skill syntax | Use `BeforeSubmitPrompt` prompt if supported syntax is confirmed. Otherwise emit nothing. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **OpenCode** | None currently, unless raw prompt has explicit skill syntax | Use turn-start prompt if supported syntax is confirmed. Otherwise emit nothing. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **Copilot CLI** | None currently, unless raw prompt has explicit skill syntax | Use `UserPromptSubmitted` prompt if supported syntax is confirmed. Otherwise emit nothing. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **Factory AI Droid** | None currently, unless raw prompt has explicit skill syntax | Use `UserPromptSubmit` when prompt exists. Exec/session-start fallback has no reliable prompt provenance. | Prompt only when explicit. |
| **External agents** | Agent-provided explicit metadata | Extend external protocol to let agents emit normalized `skill_events`. | Whatever target the external agent declares. |

## Important implementation detail

Do not only extract during post-commit condensation. Mid-turn commits can be finalized later with a fuller transcript.

So store skill events first in session state:

```txt
.git/entire-sessions/<session>.json
```

Then:

1. `TurnStart` / tool hook records `state.SkillEvents`.
2. `CondenseSession` copies relevant events into checkpoint `metadata.json`.
3. `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` must also update `skill_events` when it replaces the transcript, otherwise mid-turn checkpoints can have stale collapse metadata.

## Do not collapse on heuristics

These should not produce collapsible skill events:

- reading `SKILL.md`
- paths containing `/skills/`
- expanded prompt text containing `<skill name="...">`
- system prompt listing available skills

Only explicit runtime signals should collapse events.

content.text:
Use a confidence-tiered plan. Store every suspected skill as `skill_events[]`, but let UI collapse only above a threshold.

## Confidence levels

```txt
explicit        native structured skill event/tool
prompt_command  raw prompt starts with known skill invocation
expanded_marker transcript contains structured expansion marker
skill_file_read agent read a SKILL.md file
heuristic       weak text/path guess
```

## Per-agent plan

| Agent | Primary detection | Fallbacks | Default collapse? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Assistant `tool_use.name == "Skill"` with `input.skill` | User prompt starts with discovered Claude slash skill/command; Read tool opens `*/SKILL.md` | Yes for `Skill` tool; maybe for known slash prompt |
| **Pi** | Add Pi `input` hook; raw text starts `/skill:name` before expansion | User message contains `<skill name="...">`; read tool opens `SKILL.md` | Yes for `input`; maybe for marker |
| **Codex** | `UserPromptSubmit` prompt starts known skill/slash invocation | Transcript command reads `SKILL.md`; command output contains skill frontmatter `name:` | Yes only for known prompt command |
| **Gemini CLI** | `BeforeAgent` prompt starts known skill/slash invocation | Transcript user message starts slash; tool call reads `SKILL.md` | Yes only for known prompt command |
| **Cursor** | `BeforeSubmitPrompt` prompt starts known skill/slash invocation | Transcript user message starts slash/expanded marker | Yes only for known prompt command |
| **OpenCode** | Turn-start prompt starts known skill/slash invocation | Export transcript tool part reads `SKILL.md` | Yes only for known prompt command |
| **Copilot CLI** | `UserPromptSubmitted` prompt starts known skill/slash invocation | `events.jsonl` user message starts slash; tool telemetry mentions `SKILL.md` | Yes only for known prompt command |
| **Factory AI Droid** | `UserPromptSubmit` prompt starts known skill/slash invocation; if transcript has Claude-style `Skill` tool, use that | Assistant tool reads `SKILL.md` | Yes for `Skill` tool / known prompt |
| **External agents** | Let external protocol emit normalized `skill_events` | Generic slash/`SKILL.md` heuristics | Depends on confidence |

## Generic prompt detector

Run this on every `TurnStart` prompt:

```txt
1. exact /skill:name       → prompt_command
2. exact known invocation  → prompt_command
   e.g. /foo, /plugin:foo if discovered for that agent
3. slash-looking unknown   → heuristic
```

Known invocations come from agent discovery when available, e.g. Claude `.claude/skills`, `.claude/commands`, plugins, etc.

## Generic transcript detector

Run during condensation/finalization:

```txt
1. native Skill tool call          → explicit
2. user message starts known slash → prompt_command
3. structured skill wrapper        → expanded_marker
4. tool reads */SKILL.md           → skill_file_read
5. output/frontmatter has name     → skill_file_read with inferred skill name
```

## Collapse policy

```txt
explicit / prompt_command  => collapse by default
expanded_marker            => collapse by default only if anchor is exact
skill_file_read            => show as skill activity; maybe not collapse prompt
heuristic                  => never default-collapse
```

So even unreliable detections are preserved, but each carries `confidence`, and the UI can decide how aggressive to be.

content.text:
You're right — “run on every TurnStart” is too vague. The better plan is:

1. **Use existing hooks where they already exist.**
2. **Have each agent adapter emit `skill_events` only when it sees a skill signal.**
3. **Backfill from transcript during condensation only for agents where runtime hooks don’t expose enough.**

There *is* an existing TurnStart path:

```txt
agent hook → ParseHookEvent → agent.Event{Type: TurnStart, Prompt: ...}
          → handleLifecycleTurnStart(...)
```

But today it only captures pre-prompt state, writes `prompt.txt`, initializes session state, etc. It does **not** classify skills.

## Core design

Add:

```go
type SkillEvent struct {
	ID          string `json:"id"`
	EventType  string `json:"event_type"` // prompt_invocation | tool_invocation | skill_file_read
	SkillName  string `json:"skill_name"`
	Invocation string `json:"invocation,omitempty"`

	Agent      string `json:"agent"`
	Signal     string `json:"signal"`     // native signal used
	Confidence string `json:"confidence"` // explicit | probable | heuristic

	TurnID    string `json:"turn_id,omitempty"`
	Timestamp string `json:"timestamp,omitempty"`

	ToolUseID string `json:"tool_use_id,omitempty"`

	CollapseTarget string `json:"collapse_target"` // user_message | tool_call | tool_pair | none
	DefaultCollapse bool   `json:"default_collapse"`

	Native map[string]string `json:"native,omitempty"`
}
```

Then add:

```go
SkillEvents []agent.SkillEvent `json:"skill_events,omitempty"`
```

to session state and committed metadata.

## Per-agent plan

### Claude Code

**Best signal:** native `Skill` tool call.

Detection:

```txt
assistant content block:
  type == "tool_use"
  name == "Skill"
  input.skill != ""
```

Implementation:

- Transcript extractor in `claudecode/transcript.go`.
- Optionally install `PostToolUse` matcher for `Skill` later, but transcript extraction is enough for checkpoint metadata.

Store:

```json
{
  "event_type": "tool_invocation",
  "skill_name": "trigger-analysis",
  "agent": "claude-code",
  "signal": "skill_tool_use",
  "confidence": "explicit",
  "tool_use_id": "toolu_...",
  "collapse_target": "tool_pair",
  "default_collapse": true
}
```

Collapse: the `Skill` tool call/result pair.

---

### Pi

**Best signal:** Pi extension `input` event before skill expansion.

Pi docs say `input` fires before `/skill:name` expansion. So update `agent/pi/entire_extension.ts`:

```ts
pi.on("input", async (event, ctx) => {
  if (event.text.startsWith("/skill:")) {
    // record pending skill invocation
  }
});
```

Then include that pending event in the next `before_agent_start` hook payload.

Detection:

```txt
raw input starts /skill:name
```

Store:

```json
{
  "event_type": "prompt_invocation",
  "skill_name": "trigger-analysis",
  "invocation": "/skill:trigger-analysis",
  "agent": "pi",
  "signal": "input_slash_command",
  "confidence": "explicit",
  "collapse_target": "user_message",
  "default_collapse": true
}
```

Fallbacks:

- transcript contains `<skill name="...">` → probable
- assistant reads `SKILL.md` → heuristic/probable

---

### Codex

No known native skill event.

Use only weaker signals:

1. `UserPromptSubmit` raw prompt starts `/skill:name`
2. transcript user message starts `/skill:name`
3. transcript command/tool reads `SKILL.md`

Store with lower confidence unless syntax is confirmed.

```json
{
  "event_type": "prompt_invocation",
  "skill_name": "foo",
  "invocation": "/skill:foo",
  "agent": "codex",
  "signal": "user_prompt_submit_slash_command",
  "confidence": "probable",
  "collapse_target": "user_message",
  "default_collapse": false
}
```

Collapse only if product wants aggressive mode.

---

### Gemini CLI

Similar to Codex.

Signals:

1. `BeforeAgent` prompt starts `/skill:name`
2. Gemini transcript user message starts `/skill:name`
3. Gemini `toolCalls` read a `SKILL.md`

Default: store, but don’t auto-collapse unless confidence is high.

---

### Cursor

Signals:

1. `BeforeSubmitPrompt` prompt starts `/skill:name`
2. transcript user message starts `/skill:name`
3. possible expanded marker if Cursor exposes one later

Cursor transcripts don’t appear to expose useful skill tool calls today.

Default collapse only for explicit slash prompt.

---

### OpenCode

Signals:

1. turn-start prompt starts `/skill:name`
2. exported transcript user message starts `/skill:name`
3. tool part reads `SKILL.md`

Store `skill_file_read` separately from prompt invocation.

---

### Copilot CLI

Signals:

1. `UserPromptSubmitted` prompt starts `/skill:name`
2. `events.jsonl` `user.message` starts `/skill:name`
3. weak fallback if tool telemetry references `SKILL.md`

Probably no default collapse except exact prompt command.

---

### Factory AI Droid

Droid transcripts are Claude-like enough to support:

1. assistant tool_use `Skill` if present
2. prompt starts `/skill:name`
3. assistant reads `SKILL.md`

If `Skill` tool is present, treat like Claude:

```json
"confidence": "explicit",
"default_collapse": true
```

Otherwise store weaker signals.

---

### External agents

Extend external agent protocol to optionally return normalized `skill_events`.

If external agent supplies:

```json
{
  "skill_events": [...]
}
```

trust it as explicit. Otherwise use generic weak transcript fallbacks only.

## Key correction

Do **not** add one generic “detect skills on every TurnStart” pass.

Instead:

```txt
agent-specific hook/parser sees signal
        ↓
adds SkillEvent to agent.Event or transcript extraction result
        ↓
session state accumulates SkillEvents
        ↓
CondenseSession writes SkillEvents to metadata.json
        ↓
API/UI uses metadata to collapse events
```

So the current TurnStart path is only the transport point when the agent already gives us the prompt. The real detection stays inside each agent adapter.
Which are the safest bets?

Safest bets, in order:

1. **Claude Code `Skill` tool call**
   - Signal: assistant `tool_use.name == "Skill"` with `input.skill`.
   - This is the cleanest explicit “skill was invoked” event.
   - Safe to default-collapse the Skill tool call/result.

2. **Pi `/skill:name` via `input` extension event**
   - Signal: Pi `input` event sees raw `/skill:name` before expansion.
   - Explicit prompt-level invocation.
   - Safe to collapse the expanded skill prompt/user message.

3. **Any agent where CLI itself launches a prompt that starts with a known skill command**
   - Signal: CLI constructed the prompt or received exact raw hook prompt equal to known invocation.
   - Safe if exact and agent-specific syntax is known.

4. **Factory AI Droid if it emits Claude-style `Skill` tool calls**
   - Signal: same as Claude: `tool_use.name == "Skill"` + `input.skill`.
   - Safe only if present in real Droid transcripts.

Everything else is less safe:

- `SKILL.md` read: means skill file was loaded, but not necessarily the user prompt was a skill.
- `/skills/...` path: weak.
- `<skill name="...">`: decent for Pi expansion, but still weaker than raw `input`.
- Prompt contains `/skill:name` in stored transcript: okay-ish, but could be pasted text or post-expansion artifacts.

So I’d implement first:

```txt
Phase 1:
  Claude Code Skill tool call
  Pi raw input /skill:name

Phase 2:
  exact raw prompt command detection for agents with confirmed skill syntax

Phase 3:
  skill-file-read heuristics as non-default-collapse metadata only
```
Let's implement this as a PoC for Claude and Pi. Create a new branch and commit the changes once done. Don't stop until done.

Adds normalized `skill_events` sidecar metadata that captures when AI agents invoke native skills, without rewriting raw transcripts. Claude Code derives events from `Skill` tool-use blocks in its transcript; Pi captures `/skill:name` slash commands in the TypeScript extension and forwards them through hooks. Events flow through session state (with dedup), are merged with transcript-extracted events during condensation/finalization, and persisted to per-session checkpoint `metadata.json` with a `skill_events_version`.

- New `agent.SkillEvent` data model, `SkillEventExtractor` capability/interface, and generic `ExtractSkillEvents` helper.
- Claude transcript extraction of `Skill` tool calls (using new `ContentBlock.ID`); Pi hook payload + TS extension capture of `/skill:name` before prompt expansion.
- Lifecycle/state plumbing: `Event.SkillEvents`, session-state append+dedup, condensation/finalization merging and write into `WriteCommittedOptions`/`UpdateCommittedOptions` plus `CommittedMetadata`.

content.text:
Valid comment. Addressed it.

Changed state-level dedup so two skill events with distinct non-empty IDs are not collapsed.

New commit pushed:

```txt
b7c0dfcbb Preserve repeated skill events with distinct IDs
```

Replied on the PR thread.

Tests run:

```txt
mise exec -- go test ./cmd/entire/cli ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/pi ./cmd/entire/cli/strategy
```
"collapsed"?

I meant “deduplicated away,” not UI-collapsed.

The review comment was about this bug:

- Pi can emit two `/skill:foo` events in the same turn.
- They have different IDs/timestamps.
- Our state dedup logic could still treat them as duplicates because it fell through to a broad comparison.
- So the second event could be dropped from session state.

I fixed that so distinct event IDs are preserved.

This is separate from the metadata field:

```json
"collapse": {
  "target": "user_message",
  "default_collapsed": true
}
```

That field is just a UI hint for later.
Document the format how we are capturing a skill in the metadata.

content.text:
**Shadow branch lifecycle:**
- Created on first checkpoint for a base commit
- Migrated automatically if base commit changes (stash → pull → apply scenario)
- Deleted after condensation to `entire/checkpoints/v1`
- Reset if orphaned (no session state file exists)

### Committed Checkpoints

Branch: `entire/checkpoints/v1`

Metadata only, sharded by checkpoint ID. Supports **multiple sessions per checkpoint**:

```
<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/
├── metadata.json        # CheckpointSummary (aggregated stats)
├── 0/                   # First session (0-based indexing)
│   ├── metadata.json    # Session-specific CommittedMetadata
│   ├── full.jsonl
│   ├── prompt.txt       # Checkpoint-scoped user prompts
│   └── content_hash.txt
├── 1/                   # Second session
│   ├── metadata.json
│   ├── full.jsonl
│   └── ...
└── 2/                   # Third session...
```

**Root-level metadata.json (`CheckpointSummary`):**
```json
{
  "checkpoint_id": "abc123def456",
  "strategy": "manual-commit",
  "branch": "main",
  "checkpoints_count": 3,
  "files_touched": ["file1.txt", "file2.txt"],
  "sessions": [
    {
      "metadata": "/ab/c123def456/0/metadata.json",
      "transcript": "/ab/c123def456/0/full.jsonl",
      "content_hash": "/ab/c123def456/0/content_hash.txt",
      "prompt": "/ab/c123def456/0/prompt.txt"
    }
  ],
  "token_usage": {
    "input_tokens": 1500,
    "cache_creation_tokens": 200,
    "cache_read_tokens": 800,
    "output_tokens": 500,
    "api_call_count": 3
  }
}
```

When condensing multiple concurrent sessions:
- All sessions are stored in numbered subdirectories using 0-based indexing (`0/`, `1/`, `2/`, ...)
- Each `session_id` is assigned a stable index; subsequent writes for the same session reuse the same numbered folder
- New `session_id` values are appended at the next index, so higher-numbered folders correspond to more recently introduced sessions, not necessarily the chronologically latest activity
- `sessions` array in `CheckpointSummary` maps each session to its file paths
- `files_touched` is merged from all sessions

### Checkpoint ID Linking

The checkpoint ID is the **stable identifier** that links user commits to metadata across branches.

**Format:** 12-hex-character random ID (e.g., `a3b2c4d5e6f7`)

**Generation:**
- Generated during condensation (post-commit hook)

**Usage:**

1. **User commit trailer**:
   - `Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7` added to user's commit message
   - Added by `prepare-commit-msg` hook (user can remove)

2. **Directory sharding** on `entire/checkpoints/v1`:
   - Path: `<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/` (e.g., `a3/b2c4d5e6f7/`)
   - First 2 chars = shard (256 possible shards)
   - Remaining 10 chars = directory name

3. **Commit subject** on `entire/checkpoints/v1`:
   - Format: `Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7`
   - Makes `git log entire/checkpoints/v1` readable

**Bidirectional Lookup:**

```
User commit → Metadata:
  1. Extract "Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7" from commit message
  2. Read entire/checkpoints/v1 tree at a3/b2c4d5e6f7/

Metadata → User commits:
  Given checkpoint ID a3b2c4d5e6f7
  → Search branch history for commits with "Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7"
```

Note: Commit subjects on `entire/checkpoints/v1` (e.g., `Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7`)
are for human readability in `git log` only. The CLI always reads from the tree at HEAD.

**Example Flow:**

```
                    User creates commit
                           ↓
           prepare-commit-msg hook adds trailer
                           ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Commit on main branch:                           │
│   "Implement login feature                       │
│                                                   │
│   Entire-Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7"               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           ↓
                  post-commit hook runs
                           ↓
          Condense shadow → entire/checkpoints/v1
                           ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Commit on entire/checkpoints/v1:                 │
│   Subject: "Checkpoint: a3b2c4d5e6f7"            │
│                                                   │
│   Tree: a3/b2c4d5e6f7/                           │
│     ├── metadata.json                            │
│     │   (checkpoint_id: "a3b2c4d5e6f7")          │
│     ├── 0/                                       │
│     │   ├── full.jsonl                           │
│     │   └── prompt.txt                           │
│     └── ...                                      │
│                                                   │
│   Trailers:                                      │
│     Entire-Session: 2026-01-20-uuid              │
│     Entire-Strategy: manual-commit               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The checkpoint ID creates a **bidirectional link**: user commits can find their metadata, and metadata can find the commits that reference it.
